summary: All seven round-1 findings are genuinely closed, and I re-ran the mutation battery myself rather than taking the author's numbers on trust. Baseline 35 passed in migration.test.ts, 83 across 6 files. Confirmed kills: sanitization restricted to boards[0] → 1 fail; the deliberate Object.values(board.groups) replaced by a GROUP_IDS loop → 1 fail (`a board missing a group…`, not the 2 the author reported — the mutant dies either way); the whole `version < 8` block deleted → 7 fail; the new trailing-surrogate guard removed → 1 fail. The surrogate test is stronger than it looks: it also kills a low-surrogate range typo, a guard applied before the cap instead of after, a code-point cap, and a byte cap, so the Cyrillic and emoji boundary cases each earn their place. The freshDefaultData() extraction did not lose coverage (removing its explicit array copy → 2 fail), and the second-board test's title assertion is independently load-bearing (sanitizing titles on boards[0] only → 1 fail). The deliberately unfixed minor is honestly reported: I reproduced it exactly — reducing the `version < 8` block to `result.version = 8` still leaves 35 green — and task step 5 does verbatim mandate the block shape, so the code is right to keep it; the vacuous `not.toBe(GROUP_IDS)` that would have overclaimed it is gone, and no test name or comment in the file now asserts more than it verifies. Two new gaps surfaced under mutation that round 1 did not reach. First, the test added to close round-1 major #2 overclaims in its name: after migrateData, `groupOrder` names `orgIntentions` while `board.groups.orgIntentions` is undefined, and a Task 07-style render over that array throws — yet Task 07 is explicitly told to trust this sanitizer and not re-implement it. Second, sanitizeGroupOrder's non-array branch has no instance-identity assertion: making it hand out the exported GROUP_IDS reference leaves all 35 green, even though three sibling tests cover exactly that hazard for the other three producers of the default array.

findings.location: tests/unit/migration.test.ts:263-273 (`a board missing a group does not throw and is still repaired`)
findings.issue: The test's name and comment claim the board is repaired, but only half of it is. I ran the input through migrateData and inspected the result: groupOrder comes back ['completed','backlog','focus','inProgress','orgIntentions','delegated'] while Object.keys(groups) is ['backlog','focus','inProgress','delegated','completed'] — 'orgIntentions' is a dangling id. Mapping the result the way Task 07 will (`groupOrder.map(id => board.groups[id].taskIds)`) throws "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'taskIds')". This matters because Task 07's Dependencies section says Task 3 "supplies the sanitizer that guarantees it is a permutation of the six known ids on every load" and instructs "Do not re-implement sanitization in the component" — so Task 07 will index board.groups by every id in groupOrder without a guard. The task Description also states that a groupOrder id whose group comes back undefined "must be impossible by the time migrateData returns". The test asserts the no-throw contract correctly (that was the round-1 ask, and it kills the GROUP_IDS-loop mutant), but by calling the outcome "repaired" it hands the next task a guarantee that does not hold, which is precisely the overclaim class round 1 set out to eliminate.

The `!Array.isArray(value)` branch returns `[...GROUP_IDS]` — a fresh copy — but nothing in the suite pins that. Verified by mutation: changing it to `return GROUP_IDS as unknown as GroupId[]` leaves all 35 tests green. The suite already treats instance sharing as a first-class hazard and covers it for the three other producers of the default array — `createDefaultBoard` (line 311), and both early returns (lines 292, 301) — so a reader reasonably concludes the class is covered. The one branch left unguarded is the one that fires on the most common real damage: a v8 data.json whose board has `groupOrder: null` or no groupOrder key at all. The existing `two boards get independent groupOrder arrays` test cannot catch it, because its input is v7: the `version < 8` block supplies each board a fresh `[...GROUP_IDS]`, so sanitizeGroupOrder takes the array branch and never reaches the default path. Under the mutant, two such boards would share the exported constant's own array, and `migrateData`'s result is written straight back to data.json by loadPluginData(). Stated honestly: no consumer mutates that array in place today (moveGroup in src/ui/groupOrderUtils.ts copies, and Task 08 writes a fresh array through updateBoard), so this is a latent-regression guard rather than a live bug — but the task's edge-case note is unambiguous that a fresh copy is required "everywhere the default is produced", and this is such a place.

Round-1 minor about the unobservable `version < 8` field assignments was closed by choosing the 'record the decision' branch rather than the 'change the code' branch. I checked both halves of that choice. The reasoning is sound and I verified it against the source: task step 5 verbatim requires 'every group of every board gets title: \'\' if it has no title yet, every board gets the default order if it has no order yet, and result.version = 8. Follow the existing block style', so removing the assignments would deviate from the task, and the one-block-per-version-step invariant the Description defends is a real constraint. I also confirmed the suite no longer overclaims: reducing the block to `result.version = 8` still leaves 35 green (unchanged from round 1), and the vacuous `not.toBe(GROUP_IDS)` that would have implied otherwise is deleted. The only outstanding piece is the record itself — the decisions log contains sections for Tasks 01, 02 and 05 and none for Task 03, so nothing is written down yet. Task 03's own Post-completion checklist requires that entry.
findings.recommendation: Add the Task 03 section to the decisions log before closing the task, and make the deviation explicit rather than silent. It should state: (a) the two `=== undefined` assignments inside the `version < 8` block are unobservable through any test because the unconditional sanitization block that follows overwrites both fields on every call — reducing the block to `result.version = 8` leaves the suite fully green; (b) they are kept deliberately because task step 5 mandates the block shape and the one-block-per-version-step invariant; (c) the compensating test change is that the vacuous `not.toBe(GROUP_IDS)` assertion was removed so the suite does not imply coverage it lacks, the real instance-sharing guards being the createDefaultBoard test and the two early-return tests. Also fold in the two out-of-scope observations the task pre-authorises: `groups`/`hiddenGroups` still shared by the shallow spread in the early returns (step 7 scope note), and no guard added for a missing or non-array `result.boards` (implementation hints).

findings.issue: The task's implementation hints state 'Keep the sanitizers pure and free of side effects on their input, so the unit tests can call them directly with hostile values'. That contract is untested. Verified by mutation: making sanitizeGroupOrder normalise its argument in place and return the same instance (`value.length = 0; value.push(...order); return value`) leaves all 35 tests green. This is a change from round 1, where the equivalent mutant was caught — the round-1 fix to `groupOrder already valid and non-default` replaced the self-comparison with `sanitizeGroupOrder([...custom])`, which was the right call for that finding but happens to have been the last place a caller-owned array reached the sanitizer. Impact today is latent: the only in-repo call site is migrateData, where the argument is `board.groupOrder` itself, and Task 08 deliberately writes groupOrder to the store without sanitization ('groupOrder is written to the store without sanitization, and that is intentional'). It becomes a real bug the first time a caller passes a store-owned array.

findings.location: tests/unit/migration.test.ts:269-272 (`a board missing a group does not throw and is still repaired`)
findings.issue: The test invokes migrateData twice on the same object: once inside `expect(() => migrateData(data)).not.toThrow()` and again in `expect(migrateData(data).boards[0].groupOrder)`. migrateData mutates its input in place (`let result = data as PluginData`), so the second call operates on data the first call already repaired, and the assertion is therefore made about an idempotent re-run rather than about the first-pass repair. I could not construct a mutant that this actually masks — the two calls run identical code — so the practical cost is zero today, but it is shared state between two assertions in one test and it makes the second assertion weaker than it reads.
